title: What the homepage has to prove for a recruiting firm
metaTitle: What a recruiting firm homepage must prove
excerpt: Name the kind of role you fill, then offer a way to brief the search. A handshake photo spends the first screen on the firm, not the role.
alt: A wide city avenue with yellow taxis, tall buildings, and people on the sidewalk, a civic view rather than the role this article asks the first screen to name.
caption: A city avenue is atmosphere. A hiring manager still needs the role. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a recruiting firm homepage prove first?
faqs.answer: It should name the kind of role the firm fills, then offer a way to brief the search. A hiring manager who has been burned before is checking those two things in the opening seconds. Nielsen Norman Group's page-visit research treats the first 10 seconds as the moment people decide whether to stay.

faqs.question: Why is a handshake photo a weak hero image for a search firm?
faqs.answer: It tells the firm that the work is human, which the buyer already believes. It does not show the kind of role you fill. Use the largest image for a workplace, a scorecard, or another checkable sign of the search, and keep that image loading with the headline.

faqs.question: What should the main button on the homepage say?
faqs.answer: Use a verb that matches the next screen, such as briefing the search. The next view should ask for the role and what went wrong last time, and it should say what you will do with that note. Do not promise a shortlist before you have the role, and do not invent a reply window the team cannot keep.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?
Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results

markdown:
A recruiting firm homepage has one job for a hiring manager who has been burned before: show the kind of role you fill, and offer a way to brief the search. Nielsen Norman Group's review of page-visit research puts a clock on that job. People often leave a web page within 10 to 20 seconds, and the first 10 seconds are when they decide whether to stay. A handshake, a skyline, and a line about talent solutions spend those seconds on the firm. The buyer is trying to decide whether you fill roles like theirs.

Write the page in that order. Name the role first. Then show how a search gets briefed. Jakob Nielsen's summary of the same 2011 research is the practical rule: to earn several minutes of attention, the page has to communicate its value inside those 10 seconds. The average page visit lasts a little less than a minute, and people have time to read only about a quarter of the text. The first screen is the argument. The rest of the site is for the person who stayed.

## The two proofs, in that order

The first proof is the kind of role. A hiring manager who has already paid for a search that missed does not need a category. "Executive search" is a category. "We fill head of operations roles for independent manufacturers with one plant and a working owner" is a kind of role. The sentence should be specific enough that the wrong buyer feels it is not for them.

The second proof is the brief. The action on the first screen should say what the manager will do, not what you hope they feel. "Brief a search" is an action. "Get in touch" is a hallway. If the button opens a general contact form with no mention of the role, the first screen lied.

Put those two proofs in the first view on a phone. A role sentence. One action. One picture of the work, not the lobby. If you have a true constraint you are known for, one line of it can sit beside the action. A retained search. A shortlist of five. A written scorecard before anyone is called. Do not stack three proofs. The first 10 seconds are a harsh judgment. A crowded hero asks the visitor to do the sorting you should have done.

## Why a handshake photograph fails this buyer

A handshake photograph feels safe inside the firm. It says people meet. It says the work is human. A hiring manager who has been burned already knows the work is human. They have sat through the kickoff, the weekly update, and the apology. The photograph does not answer the question they brought: do you fill this kind of role, or do you fill every role and hope one sticks.

The picture also takes the largest place on the screen. Google's Core Web Vitals guidance treats Largest Contentful Paint as the loading measure of the main content, and a good score means that paint happens within 2.5 seconds of the page starting to load. When the largest element is a stock handshake, you spent that threshold on a picture that does not name a role. When the largest element is a photograph of the kind of workplace you recruit into, or a clear still of the scorecard you use, the same threshold protects the proof.

Reject the handshake even if the lighting is good. The failure is the subject. Replace it with something a burned buyer can check against their own company. A shop floor. A clinic desk. A product bench. A written brief with the title of the role visible. If you fill more than one kind of role, pick the one this site is for. A second kind of role can live on a later page. It should not split the first screen into a collage.

## How to name the role without writing a job ad

The homepage is not a job board, and it is not a posting for one open seat. The hiring manager is the buyer. Candidates may arrive too. The page you are writing is for the person who pays for the search.

Name the role the way that person already talks about it. Use the title they put on the requisition, the level, and the kind of company. "Plant controllers for family-owned food manufacturers" is a name. "Finance leadership across the value chain" is fog. If you truly fill three families of roles, say the three titles. Do not add a fourth sentence that tries to cover "and more."

A short list can carry the proof when the titles are the point:

- The role title, at the level you actually fill.
- The company shape: headcount band, ownership, or the operating constraint that repeats.
- What you do not fill. A negative is a gift to a burned buyer. It shows you have turned work down.

Keep each line short enough to read without a paragraph. The visitor who stays past the first half minute may read more. Nielsen's finding is that once someone has stayed on a page for about 30 seconds, there is a fair chance they stay much longer, often two minutes or more. Earn the half minute with the role. Spend the later minutes on how a search is run.

Watch the candidate path while you do this. A "see open roles" link can exist. It should not sit at the same visual rank as the brief. A hiring manager who has been burned will assume the site is for everyone, which is how the last search felt. Give candidates a quiet link. Give the buyer the action.

## What the button is allowed to promise

The action has to survive contact with the next screen. If the button says "Brief the search," the next view should ask for the role, the company, and what went wrong last time, in as few fields as you can. It should also say what you will do with that note. You will read it. You will say whether you take this kind of search. You will say what a brief conversation covers.

Do not promise a shortlist on the homepage. You do not have the role yet. Promise the next honest step. A hiring manager who has been burned is listening for overclaim. "We guarantee the hire" is a line they have already heard. "Tell us the role. We will say whether we should run the search" is a line they can test.

If you are not ready to state a reply window, do not invent one for the page. Say what the step is, and leave the clock off until the team can keep it. A missing number is better than a number the office does not honor. The same rule applies to "exclusive network" and "off-market candidates." If you cannot explain the claim in one concrete sentence, it does not belong above the action.

The same action can repeat at the end of the page. In the first screen, once is enough. A second button with a different verb splits attention. Pick the brief. Let everything else be a text link.

## What belongs under the first screen

Under the first view, teach the person who stayed. How a search starts. What you need from the hiring manager before you talk to anyone. What you will not do, such as spraying a role across a database and calling it a search. One story with a constraint, a decision, and the kind of role. A short note on fees only if you are willing to show the shape. If the fee is a conversation, say that, and point to the page that explains the shape.

Each section should add a fact the hero did not. Repeating "we know talent" in softer words does not count. The visitor who stayed can tell.

A useful order is short:

1. The kind of role, already said, now with two examples.
2. How a search is briefed, and what you refuse.
3. One story of a search with a real constraint.
4. Who does the work, by name and function.
5. The brief again.

Skip an industry cloud, a counter of placements, and a carousel of logos you cannot discuss. A burned buyer treats a number with no definition as decoration. If you publish a number, define the period and the kind of role. "Forty retained searches in plant leadership over three years" is a number. "Five hundred placements" is a drum.

## How to test the page with a skeptic

You can test this in an afternoon. You do not need a panel.

Open the page on a phone. Show it to someone who hires, and who did not help write the site. Give them about ten seconds. Hide it. Ask what kind of role the firm fills, and what they would do if they had a role to brief. If they say "recruiting" and "contact us," the page has not proved either thing.

Then leave the page open and ask what they would distrust. Listen for the handshake, the skyline, the word "bespoke," and any claim of speed you cannot keep. Change the sentence or the picture. Do not add a paragraph below to compensate. People who leave in the first 10 seconds do not scroll to a disclaimer.

Three skeptics are enough if they miss the same thing. If two of them name a role you do not actually want, the sentence is too broad. Narrow it. The cost of a narrower homepage is fewer wrong briefs. That is a cost you want.

## When the homepage is still a brochure

A few patterns show up once the test is honest.

The firm fills many kinds of roles and will not choose. The page then reads as a directory. Choose the role this site is for, and let other practices sit on inner pages with their own sentences. The firm is proud of relationships and keeps leading with two people shaking hands. Replace the picture before you rewrite the headline a fourth time. The firm has a real method and hides it under identical steps. Name the step a burned buyer can check.

If the first screen names the role and the brief, the next question is the fee. A hiring manager who has been burned will look for the price as soon as the role feels familiar. Read [how to show the shape of a search fee](/blog/a-pricing-page-for-a-recruiting-firm) before you hide that shape behind a form.

When you want to see how a first screen can carry a specific offer, look at [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The useful examples are pages that name the work before they name the mood.
